opus-5.5.text:
I think the data wall is real, but it's often misunderstood. People imagine one day we simply run out of internet text and progress stops. What's actually happening is that the marginal value of more natural data keeps falling. The high-quality human-written tokens are largely used up, and adding more of the long tail doesn't give the same gains it did a few years ago. So if you keep doing pretraining the old way, yes, the pace slows.

But I don't see that as the end of scaling. It's a shift in what we scale. For the first phase of large models, the bottleneck was compute and the data was more or less free: you crawled the web and that was your fuel. Now the scarce resource is data that actually teaches the model something new. I think there are a few ways through.

The first is reinforcement learning. When you give a model a task with a verifiable outcome, like a math problem, a piece of code that has to pass tests, or an agent task that either succeeds or fails, the model generates its own training signal. It explores, makes mistakes, and learns from the reward. You're no longer limited by how much humans have written down. You're limited by how many good environments and reward signals you can build. That's a very different scaling curve, and I think we're still early on it.

The second is synthetic data, but done carefully. Naively training a model on its own outputs can collapse into something bland. The key is to have some external check, like a verifier, a tool, or an environment, so the synthetic data is actually better than what the model could produce before. Then it becomes a kind of self-improvement loop rather than an echo chamber.

The third is efficiency: getting more out of each token. Better architectures, better optimizers, better data selection. If you can learn twice as much from the same data, that's equivalent to doubling your data. People underestimate how much room is left there.

So my view is that the data wall changes the shape of progress rather than stopping it. The companies that keep improving fastest will be the ones that figure out how to turn compute into new, useful data, whether through RL, agents interacting with real environments, or long-horizon reasoning. In a sense, the model has to start producing its own experience instead of only reading ours. I think that transition is the most important thing happening in the field right now.

r001.rationale: The response links the data wall to efficiency, saying that getting more learning from each token can offset limited data.

r002.rationale: It says progress slows when using the old pretraining approach and argues progress can continue through other methods; it does not state that the pace of model improvement has not slowed.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the data wall is real, but people often misread what it means. For the first phase of scaling, we were essentially riding on the internet: trillions of tokens of human text that nobody had to produce on purpose. That reservoir is mostly consumed now, at least the high-quality part. So if you define progress as "pretrain on more human text," then yes, the pace slows down.

But I don't think that's the right definition anymore. What actually matters is whether the model can keep learning, and there are at least two directions where the ceiling is still far away.

The first is reinforcement learning. Once a model is strong enough to attempt a task, verify a result, and get a signal back, you no longer depend on someone having written the answer down somewhere. The model generates its own experience. Math, code, agentic tasks with checkable outcomes — these are domains where the effective data supply is almost unlimited, because it comes from interaction rather than from a corpus. The bottleneck shifts from "how much text exists" to "how good is your environment and your reward."

The second is efficiency. We're still far from extracting everything from the data we already have. A human reads a textbook once and gets most of the value; a model needs many passes and still misses structure. So better architectures, better training objectives, better use of long context — these are all ways of getting more intelligence per token, which is another way around the wall.

So my honest view is: the data wall ends one paradigm, but it also forces the industry to move into the next one faster. If anything, it's clarifying. It tells you that compute alone won't carry you, and the teams that win will be the ones that figure out how models create their own data and learn more from less. That's a harder problem than just scaling, but it's a much more interesting one.

r001.rationale: The response presents efficiency as a way around the data wall, describing better training and architectures as ways to get more intelligence per token.

r002.rationale: It says progress from pretraining on more human text slows down, but does not state that the overall pace of model improvement has not slowed.

astra-6.text:
I think the data wall changes how we improve models, but it doesn’t necessarily mean improvement stops. If we rely only on pretraining on more human-written text, then the supply of useful data becomes a constraint. You can’t assume that scaling the same recipe will keep giving you the same returns.

The interesting question is whether models can generate new learning experiences. In coding or mathematics, for example, a model can try different approaches and get feedback on whether they work. That gives you a way to improve beyond simply imitating existing text. But generating more tokens isn’t enough—the feedback has to distinguish a genuinely better solution from a plausible-looking one.

So I would expect progress to become more uneven. In areas where we can verify results, there’s a clearer path to continued improvement. In areas where quality is harder to measure, the data constraint may be more significant. The bottleneck shifts from how much text you have to how effectively you can turn computation and feedback into learning.

r001.rationale: The response says reliance on more human-written pretraining data is constrained and discusses learning from feedback, but it does not identify improving token efficiency as the motivation.

r002.rationale: It says improvement does not necessarily stop and predicts continued progress in some areas, but does not state that the pace of improvement has not slowed despite the data wall.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the data wall changes how we improve models, but it doesn’t necessarily mean improvement stops. If we rely only on collecting more text from the internet, that approach will eventually become harder to scale. The question is whether we can get more learning from the data we already have, and create new learning signals through interaction, feedback, and verification.

For example, in coding or mathematics, a model can generate a solution and then check whether it works. That creates an opportunity to learn beyond simply imitating existing text. But synthetic data alone isn’t a complete answer—you need a reliable way to distinguish better outputs from worse ones, otherwise you can reinforce mistakes.

So I would expect progress to become less dependent on raw data volume and more dependent on the efficiency of learning and the quality of feedback. The pace could become uneven, especially in areas where verification is difficult, but I wouldn’t view the data wall as a hard ceiling on model capability.

r001.rationale: The response discusses getting more learning from existing data and improving learning efficiency, but it does not identify token efficiency as the goal or motivation.

r002.rationale: The response says the data wall is not a hard ceiling, but it does not observe that model improvement has not slowed; it says progress could become uneven.
